title: Data and Sources
text: Billboard Hot 100 weekly charts, 2 August 1958 to 29 May 2021. The data comes from TidyTuesday (14 September 2021), which redistributes a dataset compiled by Sean Miller from Billboard.com charts (via Data.World). Each row is one song in one week’s chart: 327,895 rows covering 29,389 unique songs. Variables include the chart date, position, song title, performer, and weeks on chart. The TidyTuesday release also includes Spotify audio features for each song; these were not used in this project.

title: Data and Sources
text:
How the data was processed
All processing is done in R and can be reproduced from this project’s repository.

Download (R/01_download.R): reads billboard.csv directly from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository. The raw file (about 45 MB) is not stored in the repository; this script retrieves it.
Clean (R/02_clean.R): collapses weekly rows into one row per song, identified by TidyTuesday’s song_id (song title + performer), and saves a small processed file (data/processed/songs.rds) used by every figure.

For each song, the following measures were computed:







Measure
Definition




Total weeks on chart
Number of weeks the song appeared on the Hot 100, summed across all chart runs, including re-entries


Weeks in the Top 40
Number of weeks the song was ranked No. 40 or higher


Peak position
Best (lowest-numbered) chart position reached


Debut year
Year of the song’s first week on the chart


Top 10 hit
Song peaked at No. 10 or higher



Analysis window: songs that debuted between 1959 and 2019 (n = 28,122). Songs from 1958 were excluded because the chart began partway through that year. Songs debuting in 2020 or later were excluded because the data ends in May 2021, before many of their chart runs had finished. For the distribution figures, songs were grouped into three periods (1959–1990, 1991–2004, 2010–2019); songs debuting 2005–2009 were left out of that comparison as a transition period between the two discontinuities.

title: Data and Sources
text:
Sources

Billboard Hot 100 data: TidyTuesday, 2021-09-14
Introduction of the 1991 recurrent rule: Waxy.org, “The Whitburn Project: One-Hit Wonders and Pop Longevity”
2025 recurrent rule changes: Billboard, “Older Hits Will Now Drop Off the Hot 100 Faster”

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
text:
Is popular music becoming more disposable? In the era of short-form content, short attention spans and Tik-tok virality, I am sure we’ve all despised songs that we have had to hear 3000 times a day and collectively banished them from our social media feeds, and hence, the charts too. A common assumption about the streaming era is that songs now rise and vanish faster than ever. Using every weekly Billboard Hot 100 chart from 1958 to 2021, covering 28,122 songs that debuted between 1959 and 2019, this project asks how long songs actually stay on the chart.
At first, the data seem to confirm it. The typical song’s chart run grew from about 7 weeks in the 1960s to 20 weeks in 2001, then collapsed to 4 weeks by 2019.
But the distribution behind that trend reveals two artificial “walls”. From 1991, a quarter of all songs left the chart at exactly 20 weeks, because Billboard began removing songs after 20 weeks once they fell below No. 50. In the 2010s, more than a quarter of songs charted for a single week, mostly album tracks that entered briefly on release-week downloads and streams and never reached the top half of the chart. The apparent rise and fall in longevity therefore reflects chart rules and release patterns as much as listening habits.
Measured in a way neither wall affects, by counting how long Top 10 hits stay in the Top 40, the trend reverses: the biggest hits have grown steadily more durable, from about 10 weeks in the 1960s to more than 24 weeks in the 2010s.
The Hot 100 has not become more disposable. It has become more top-heavy: songs stay longer in the top half and come and go quick in the bottom half.
(I was inspired by https://pudding.cool/2024/11/love-songs/ to look at the Billboard dataset. Being a musician myself, this dataset sparked curiosity!)

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?: Changes in Longevity of Songs over Time
text:
A common claim about the streaming era is that popular music has become more disposable: songs rise quickly and are forgotten just as fast. Weekly Billboard Hot 100 charts allow this claim to be examined over six decades. I collapsed 327,895 weekly chart entries into one data point per song and measured each song’s longevity as its total number of weeks on the chart, including re-entries, for the 28,122 songs that debuted between 1959 and 2019.
Figure 1 shows the median chart run by year of debut. Longevity rose steadily for four decades, from roughly 7–9 weeks in the 1960s to a peak of 20 weeks for songs debuting in 2001, before falling sharply to a median of 4 weeks in 2019. Taken at face value, this trajectory supports the disposability claim. However, the distribution around the median suggests that this reading is incomplete: from 1991 onward, the upper quartile is fixed at almost exactly 20 weeks, a ceiling that coincides with a change in the way Billboard assigned these rankings. We examine this pattern in the following section.








Figure 1: Median number of weeks spent on the Billboard Hot 100, by year of chart debut (N = 28,122 songs, 1959–2019). The shaded band shows the interquartile range (25th–75th percentile). Weeks are counted across all chart runs, including re-entries. The dashed line marks the 1991 introduction of Billboard’s recurrent rule, which removes songs from the chart after 20 weeks once they fall below No. 50.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?: Changes in Longevity of Songs over Time
section: Two discontinuities in the distribution of chart runs
text:
Two discontinuities in the distribution of chart runs
Medians summarise the centre of a distribution but can ignore some important patterns. Figure 2 therefore shows the full distribution of chart-run lengths for songs debuting in three periods: before the 1991 methodology change (1959–1990), after the change but before digital downloads became widespread (1991–2004), and the download and streaming era (2010–2019). Songs debuting 2005–2009 are omitted as a transition period.
Before 1991, chart runs follow a smooth, right-skewed distribution: runs of exactly 20 weeks account for 2% of songs, no different from neighbouring lengths. Among songs debuting in 1991–2004, 25% leave the chart at exactly 20 weeks. This discontinuity links to Billboard’s recurrent rule, introduced in 1991, which removes a song from the Hot 100 once it has charted for 20 weeks and fallen below No. 50. This was done to make space for newer songs by getting rid of the bottom half of songs that have charted for a long time.
A second discontinuity appears in 2010–2019, when 28% of songs (1,245 of 4,446) spend a single week on the chart, compared with 3% before 1991. They reflect a release pattern in which tracks from newly released albums briefly enter the chart on first-week downloads or streams. Together, these two features account for much of the trajectory in Figure 1. The rise in median longevity after 1991 coincides with a policy-imposed ceiling, while the decline after 2005 is driven largely by a growing mass of single-week entries at the bottom of the chart.








Figure 2: Distribution of total weeks on the Billboard Hot 100 for songs debuting in three periods. Bars show the share of each period’s songs with a given chart run; runs longer than 40 weeks are not shown. Black bars mark runs of exactly 1 and exactly 20 weeks, with their shares labelled. Songs debuting 2005–2009 are omitted as a transition period.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?: Changes in Longevity of Songs over Time
section: Top hits have grown more durable
text:
Top hits have grown more durable
I then restricted the analysis to songs that peaked in the Top 10 (n = 4,837) and measured how many weeks each spent in the Top 40. The rule of getting rid of songs that spent more than 20 weeks on the chart applies only to songs below No. 50, and single-week entries almost never reach the Top 10: of the 1,245 one-week songs debuting in 2010–2019, only one did.
Figure 3 compares this measure with the all-song median from Figure 1. The two series track each other closely until the early 2000s, then diverge. While the median song’s total chart run fell, Top 10 hits continued to grow more durable. Consistent with longer stays at the top, fewer songs reached the Top 10 each year, falling from an average of about 106 per year in the 1960s to about 52 per year in the 2010s.
Taken together, the three figures suggest that the Hot 100 has not become uniformly more disposable. The bottom of the chart now turns over faster than at any point in its history, but the songs at the top remain there longer than ever. Apparent trends in chart longevity depend substantially on how the chart itself is constructed.
Further examination of the data and research into Billboard’s ranking methods may give us insight into the reason behind these trends which might be much deeper than the advent of streaming platforms.








Figure 3: Median weeks by year of chart debut for two measures. Dashed grey: total weeks on the chart for all songs (as in Figure 1). Solid black: weeks spent in the Top 40 for songs that peaked in the Top 10 (n = 4,837). The Top 40 measure is unaffected by the recurrent rule, which applies only below No. 50, and by one-week entries, which rarely reach the Top 10. Dotted line: 1991, when the recurrent rule was introduced and Billboard began using Nielsen SoundScan sales and BDS airplay data.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
text:
It feels like songs come and go faster than ever. A track blows up on TikTok, everyone streams it for a week, and then it’s gone. The Billboard Hot 100 has ranked America’s most popular songs every week since 1958, so we can check whether that feeling is true.
I looked at 28,122 songs that hit the chart between 1959 and 2019 and asked a simple question: how long did each one stay?

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
section: At first glance, yes: songs are vanishing faster
text:
At first glance, yes: songs are vanishing faster
In the 1960s, a typical song spent about 7 weeks on the Hot 100. That number climbed for 40 years, to a high of 20 weeks in 2001. Then it crashed. By 2019, the typical song lasted just 4 weeks.
Hover over the line to see any year.








Figure 1




Case closed? Not quite. Something odd is hiding underneath that line.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
section: But two “walls” in the data weren’t built by listeners
text:
But two “walls” in the data weren’t built by listeners
Instead of looking at the typical song, let’s count how many songs lasted exactly 1 week, exactly 2 weeks, and so on. If people simply lose interest at different times, you’d expect a smooth curve. That’s exactly what we see before 1991.
After that, two strange walls appear.








Figure 2





The 20-week wall is a rule. In 1991, Billboard started removing any song that had been on the chart for 20 weeks once it dropped below No. 50, to make room for new music. Songs didn’t stop being popular at week 20. Billboard stopped counting them. This was to make space for new songs as people seemed to get quite attached to songs they liked. But if they weren’t too great (so below top 50), Billboard got rid of them to make space for newer songs to shine.
The one-week wall is about how music is released now. When a big artist drops an album, many of its tracks get streamed enough to chart in the first week, then fall off. Nine in ten of them never make it into the top half of the chart.
So that first chart was measuring Billboard’s rules and album release days as much as what people actually liked.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
section: The biggest hits are lasting longer than ever
text:
The biggest hits are lasting longer than ever
Here’s a fairer test. Take only the songs that became real hits by reaching the Top 10, and count how long they stayed in the Top 40. Neither wall touches this: the 20-week rule only removes songs below No. 50, and one-week album tracks almost never reach the Top 10.
Hover over either line to compare years.








Figure 3




The two lines move together for decades, then split apart. The typical song now disappears in a few weeks, but the biggest hits are staying near the top longer than ever: about 10 weeks in the 1960s, 26 weeks by 2019.

title: Are Hit Songs Getting More Disposable?
section: So, are hits getting more disposable?
text:
So, are hits getting more disposable?
No, but the chart has changed shape. The bottom of the Hot 100 now churns faster than ever, with dozens of songs passing through for a single week. The top has become stickier: the songs everyone really listens to stay there for months.
Whether music looks “disposable” depends on which songs you count and on rules most listeners never hear about.
